evidence.title: Explainable AI for Equitable Nurse Scheduling: Pragmatic Pre-Post Implementation Study

commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-eight studies, all but one in simulated settings, suggest that explanations can raise clinician trust and confidence and sometimes accuracy, but several found that explanations increased acceptance of wrong AI output or lowered accuracy depending on format and user expertise. No study tested whether explanations help clinicians explain recommendations to patients or change patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Only one test (pmid:42391503) came from a real deployment, and it lacked a comparator and measured satisfaction. The randomized trials used simulated cases, often with students, and measured trust or accuracy on vignettes. Results are inconsistent across formats. The 2020-assessment radiology trial appears in two reports, epmc:PPR986843 and pmid:42026140, and should be counted once.

Explanations may amplify errors when the AI is wrong. Visual explanations lowered accuracy by 33.6% on misleading cases (pmid:40533485), and heatmaps dropped student accuracy from 63.3% to 50.7% (pmid:40344152). Physicians did not look longer at explanations for unsafe recommendations (pmid:39992918). SHAP explanations lowered understanding of wrong recommendations for 17% of professionals (pmid:41550460).

Format and user expertise appear to shape the effect. Chain-of-thought text improved radiologist accuracy by 12.2 points versus control (pmid:42026140). Annotated advice helped non-experts but not radiologists (pmid:36697450). General practitioners without technical backgrounds found current visualizations of limited value (pmid:40775927). Clinicians reported that explanations mattered less as their familiarity and expertise grew (pmid:42066251).

In the one live deployment, 82 of 156 nurses (52.6%) regularly engaged with SHAP explanations (pmid:42391503), which suggests uptake may be partial. Pulmonologists asked that explanation depth be tailored to expertise (pmid:38633019). Tailoring would add design and maintenance work for each user group, and no study reported its cost.

The recommendation aims to help clinicians explain AI output to patients, yet no study measured clinician-patient communication, patient understanding, or patient trust. One vignette study found that explainability raised clinician trust (β=.508) and also raised perceived professional identity threat (β=.351) (pmid:40138691). That second effect may influence how clinicians discuss AI with patients.

All tests enrolled clinicians or students, and none reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. The evidence therefore cannot show whether explanations help clinicians communicate AI results to patients who face language or literacy barriers.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested explanations in live clinical use with a comparator, measured decision quality when the AI was wrong in real care, or assessed whether explanations improve clinicians' ability to explain recommendations to patients. Comparative trials in deployed settings that measure patient understanding and outcomes by explanation format and clinician expertise are needed.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and most did not report the care setting. Any benefit or harm of explanations for clinician communication with these patients is untested.
